"Not in the slightest," I continued : "and to relieve 'your mind from its speculative burden alto my position life I may state I ant a rtudent nature, and grateful bar any information of the habits, customs, &co of any living creature, from a comu.ou mould worm to the apex of nature—man." "I'm jes the cove not can give you a fair slice, then," said Like keeper ; 'none o' your sliamblin• Sunday go-as. you-nlease sort here. No, no; not by a bucketful. Do you know, I've a tarnation hatred against theman who'd sling the basket under Ws aria, with a paper bag in his hand, and leading %bleary-eyed. crank-tailed mop of a dog. Such a stench-pot, middeieref use, offal-col-human- nature sort o' fellow would rather spank a few miles with such an animal than give his own child five minutes' airing. zoo's, nue "Them 'ere animals," lie said, pointing to a healthy- looking range of kennels, 'nee properly fed, cleaned, and cared for; and there's not a single four-legged inhabitant but wot would lay down its life for roe. Keep a respectable distance. sir ; they're dead on strangers. What breed is that? It's a lop-ear'd Hibernian spaniel. Cute fellew; knowing ass Christian, and full o' mischief as an ape. Fight? No, bless you, never gets his coat torn in a atreet brawl. A perfect general he is; believes in lying around waiting for an opportunity. I took him for an airing a few weeks back to the poat with a ratchet o' lett-rs, when an ornary looking, square-jaw'd, chubby- beaded bulldog came careering around wanting a bit of close conversation, you see; but *Cyclops '—that's his name—had him gauged up in a crack. He knew for a dead certainty that the squarojaw'd fellow wanted to mop somethirg up, and jet' squatted down on the pave- ment, cool as an iceberg, with hin forepaws on tlie satchel and his eyes working like a mortar-mill as the other dog kept circling round and round, coming closer and closer, and jot' as the orbary-looking brute was going to pop the first question, *Cyclops* sudden-like snapped, seizing him fly the hinder leg and holding on like a vice. Ler, but there was an opera, atarting at the top C and , running up. I jot' gave an approving nod, and • Cyclops,' sorry like, dripped the damaged log, and the chubby- boasted fellow went limping away like a cart with a side- I spring broke. ; "That 'ere dog, you mean? That's a Maltese terrier, the nastiest cro.A-tempered animal that ever chasol ma 1 chorus o' ists—true ti the core, mind you; stand. to / duty likes soldier. Jeb' show that fellow a rat run, an : he'll empty that burrower bell be paralysed. Sit on it like • limpet to a crag, no he will. Nover saw a rat bunt, 1 didn't you? Then you've a treat in st;:re. Out on the ; water's edge, or in some tarn with tbe itaT plyered ; like a riddle, a oeiple :if ferrets or so, and ' Dragon ' 1 there uy your side, then brace op 305 r nether garments, ; and you are in for a day. No scauipin' his work, des' sit there quit•t and or'intry biting, waiting for the *bust / up,' and then for the fun. Mont always comes out with / his mouth like a slaughter-house. Best boy ever I clapped eyes on fir evicting tenants. Ni leaving 'ern by the wayside to kick out. Jes' one hanch, and they're ready for the undertaker. "Fine animal that, you say? Ay, ay ; but that's the 1 Pride 0' the [lack, the ma.ster'e heart's own *Emperor,' , and he bears the name with as much dignity nuns arch-1 tishop does his cowl. What countryman is he? A ; ,• Newfoundland, with quite a heap o' medals for saving ; life. Plunge into the water liken seal, and seize a ten- 1 stone bump o humanity by the nape .0' the neck, and haul it on shore like a Briton. No milks; no Wain' in a corner with that fellow when "Man overboard" is heard, 1 like many of your cowardly duel aria who'd stand by the brink of a lake while a child went down a third time, and make no effort to save it. No, sir; the word Duty rings in his ears like a convent bell as he takes a ' header,' and, good Samaritan like, keeps Hs* poor soul's breathing pert above *he water line until it be safely landed. Thrre'g unselfi,ll patriotism, devotion to duty, . for you that darkens the lamps n' the likes o' you and me, who sneeringly carry ciur heads above the, inches o' starch, and with the delicate fingers e' vanity pat the forehead o' contempt and puff OIitrAVPS up Ira the fore- moat enlightened place under the stars. Faugh! Bah! Holy horrors! but Din winding on a lot o' bad temper, and I don't want to, because nll showing yea the traits of these noble animals.

I stood sponsor to that fellow's name, Gip:the most restless, uniwoy little urchin that ever yelped for his milk. What breed r did you say? Oh, he's an English terrier, gains right up to the dozen: Bowe oft rats like steam, but awfully dead on cats. Can't bear the smell of a far-listed cloak. Any • mhow-llowin" going on in the ntighbourhood, and kin bristles are up, snapping, growling, and clanking his chains something furious. I Oh, yes, there'd be no end o' lumber if he had the I bracelets off. . . . . .

Here we are landed, as the outing in. A beauty, isn't it? My lady's favourite, e Poppy." Hung me if I can sort out his geneaology somehow. fle's a mongrel-bred pug, wiinething between a nigger and a Chinaman. harm- less as a kitten and as pettish as a spoiled child, fed with cokes, jam, awl a Turkish bath now and again. I wonder he hasn't the gout. Perfectly appalling it is to ' tee the food be kicks over. Ah, I could—but if he happens to net up a melancholy whine, lee! but isn't there a bustle. 'Me dawg ! My daws ! Jim, hurry up and fetch the vet. oh once. Poppy's in distress.' And I'm jerked off a couple o' miles tor the canine doctor, when a black draught is about the best medicine we could give him. e Them are a philanthropical • Holy Friar sort o' animal of the St. Bernard breed; more real human nature bottled up in them 'ere dogs than in many a con- gregation. Out on the trackless snow, up the monntain Side, through the forest, or down in the valley, in search of the at traveller on the point of making his winding- sheet under the blue sad the stars, and, once found, they stand by him faithful as the penitent e the cress, lapping his void lace with their tongue, occasionally giving ups dismal howl until assistance arrives and the perishing traveller is rescued from his sow-bound bed. Gramercy, but they be real angel. I feels downright !sorry when I think o' the poor little orphan with- out a friend or relative in the world with the scanty rags n' poverty hanging from his thin, feeble body, and driven to find a night's shelter from the withering winter blast in the cold, damp clammy niche of a railway ark. I There are the humanitarians? Where the St. Bernards of aociety ? A child is here. Ood's image, bared to the cold and cheerless canopy of heaven, in a dying condition ; a loving mother's name is affectionately lisped from his blanched lips; his voice is failing, his eyes beemning waxen. Haste ! What! Will you, you bundle of passions in human form, contemptibly deign to scorn him because of his lowly birth? You, you scorpion, you poisonous adder, you dungeon vapour, whose slimy conceit has cooled down the fires of humanity and left you little above the wild beast—nut on you, you moral Bend. and honest humanity will write your epitaph as It deserves. But, there, vs BYO, ET at summer heat again; most always am when I think on these ques- tbins. No, sir, thanks, never taken any perquisites, shall always feel glad when you're around these quarers if you drops in and bass chat with Old Jim, the kennel keeper.

SATURDAY, APRIL 27, 1889.

The LORD SALISBURY made many Ira-jars speeches at 13ristoloin Tuesday, but he haul not much to say. lie is afraid of doing anything that will help on reform, and Wlaaaaaaipaaliticiail lIRS 111/ policy of his own it is Si) DOUAI grinding of the wind to incessantly criti- cise the probable policy of a probable successor. It will be satisfactory to Liberals to observe that the proposal whit-la has been discussed to provide a Home Rule Parliament for each of the four ountrns, namely, England, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales, may he soul to have advanced It stage in that it is honoured with the opposition of a Tory Prime Minister. We have hope flow of its ultimate adoption. All great reform proposals pa. 3 thniugh three distinct stages : in the first stage they are treated with indilierencs: ; in the second they are opposed by the Tories and in the third they arc adiipted lay Parliament. "Mane Rule all round- has reached the semild stage: Lord SALISBURY opposes it, and that means that in the end it will Imo.° the law of the land. It is suggestive of lain lordship's helplessness on the Irish unestion that lie cannot think of anything better than trying to frighten people with the bogey of Mune Rule—just as if the electors were so many timorous children. Assuming that Ireland ! had a Parliament of her own, he sells:—" Is there any impediment to prevent them in the case. let us suppose, of some European war, where you might be fighting for your existence—is them any- thing to prevent the Government of an indepen- dent Ireland, or an Ireland practically indepen- dent, from placing those splendid harbours winch lie opposite to you here at the disposal of a foreign fleet?" Our anewer is that there I

.• would be a great deal more in the nature of prevention with florae Rule than without it. If treachery were attempted at all, it would be attempted by people bitter at heart against England through the wrongs of centuries and the sufferings of to-day. But Home Hide would put ail 0101 to that bitter feeling. :aid remove the causes of sabring. Ireland could in ease of invasion be canted on to fight for us instead of against us. It is Coercion, always Coercion, which makes Ireland asource of danger; it is the employment if the battering-rain, and the shooting down of citizens when they meet to discuss their grievances which drive maddened men to think of foreign aid. Make Ireland one with England by giving her equal laws and treat- ing her generally as an Espial, awl Irishmen will be as eager as Englishmen to guard the land of their birth.

As regards the promise of Local Government for Ireland, Lord SALISBURY leaves it pretty clear that nothing is to be done just yet to redeem the plmlge. Indeed, he has the hardihood to say : " We never pledged ourselves to do it immedi- ately wo pledged ourselves to do it as oppor- tunity might serve, and as the conditions of Ireland might suit such an experiment." His lordship forgets, or perhaps we shoold say ignores, the deliberate engagement of Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL, when he was the mouthpiece in the House of Commons of Lord SALISBURY'S Govern- . meet. He promised, and he has stated that he had the aothority of the Cabinet for the promise, that whenever Local Government was given to England Ireland should also be dealt with. There sheuld, to use his own words, be "similarity and simultaneity " ; and in view of this notorious fact we accuse Lord SALISBURY of a gross breach at faith which he is trying to hide by gross mendacity. He shrinks the issue to-day by an empty promise to introduce "some mown-0" after Ireland has heel" a long spell of firm, impartially administered law.- In other words, instead of "equal laws,- the Irish are to have "a long spell" of batons, bayonets, and battering-rams. And what of the promised meanure which is now hinted at only ? Is it sug- gested that it will be on the lines of the Loud Government Act for this country? Not a bit of it. If Lord SALISBURY has his way, it will be a mean and miserable piece of class legislation. In the first place, he says We are perfectly resolved that we will not, knowing it, aid in the passing il inything that will give them a leverage, 1,5 ohtain Home Rule;" and then he adds as to this power, which is not to be used RS a leverage, that he " would much rather see it in the hands of a !comber of freeholders who could take an independent view of their position." This points to a limited franchise, to a wretched attempt to pid local government not in the hands of the ortjority, hut in the hands of the minority. not the day Tory trickery of this kind is lost. Lord SIMSBURY may be able ta block the way for a tiele; Ina he will find himself unahle to palm off a Act of fancy franchises upon the people of Ireland. We suspect that nit even Liberal Unionists wonld stand that ; the sham would he r,N) transpired.

Churchill We are beginning to feel sorry for and Mr. (*HA MRSRLAIN : he conies out of everything so badly —since he left the Liberal party. There was a time when he Icould, in II struggle, throw Lord itt NDOLPH CIIVISCHILL without once taking wind ; hut as things go to-day his lordship lays hioi nit WY I back and be is helpless. No mm who reads the charming bow letters lietween "My Dear Chamberlain " eel" My Dear Churchill" can fail to perceive that the member for West Birming- ham cuts a sorry figure. It is the Tory leader who uses the sludge hammer, and every blow makes its inark. Mr. CHAMBEIMAIN is not , exactly told that bin word is not taken, but he is informed that the man whose word lie disputes " is incapable of making as assertion contrary to facts within his own knowledge." list Lord Randolph's hardest hit is delivered as follows " Suppose this great Tory party WM to test the ! arithmetical :SLIM Of the resolution of the Liberal Unionist Association to which I have alludA, on the point as to which party hi Bir- mingham fielteinel the preponderance of pmuhitical power; suppose they decided to run candi- dates of theirown in all divisions of Birming- ham, I do not know who would have the best of it—they or the repeal party. But this is certain, that you and your friends would be politically annihilated." Mr. CHASIBRIALAIN when he read this from the friend, who along with himself, was to be a buttress of the " Brest National Party." oh, that it should come to this—that even RANDOLPH call jeer at his fallen fortunes ! All that the member for West Birmingham can say in reply—and this " with bated breath awl whispered humbleness" —is that if a joint canvass wore niude he believes that it would " show that the Conservative party is weaker and Liberal Unionists stronger than has hitherto been supposed." Touching the main cause of the family quarrel at Birmingham, there can be no doubt, from all the correspondence that has heen published, that the Tories and the Liberal Unionmisto did enter into a compact as to a Tory being put forward for the Central Division— & compact mule, let it he understood, whilst Joss BRICHE, the greatest of Liberal Unionists, was lying on a sick bed. But Mr. CHAMORRLAIN was careful that his hand shmild not Im seen; lie let others pull the strings, so that he might at the right moment pall them another way; for he dis- liked the idea of having such a brother as CHUR- CHILL SO ricer the throne. And now even Unionists smite him for his conduct, and he meekly kisses the rod. Pmir JeSSSII! He w. a Sinuses, Inn he has been shorn of his strength through toying with the Delilah of Toryism.

Mr. Henry Harrison, of Oxford, was imprisoned last week for daring to give food to starving tenants in Ireland. In the first instance he was arrested on the charge of making forcible entry into a house he was returned for trial on the charge of inciting to maintain forcible possession , arid at ten o'clock ,m Monday night the authori- I ties had abandoned Imth chargim, and served him ! with a summons on the charge of conspiracy as co-defendant with Mr. Conyheare. On Tuesday the programme was again varied ; he was allowed to go free under an adjournment. And this is how "law " is administered in Ireland !

Mr. Herman-Hodge, the member for the Accrington Division of Lancashire, like other Tory candidates, scouted the idea of Lord Salisbury re- sorting to coercion. Replying in July Dein to a speech made by the Upend candidate. he ob- served : - -" Mr. Leese said that if the Tories were put into power, the Government would go back to ispereion. That was a very wicked thing, to say." If very wicked to suggest such a thing what must it he to hack it up by votes as Mr. Herman-Hodge has done That is the question which his consti- tuents ore now asking him; ltud he has no answer to it. He stands convicted of breach if faith.

• TRACHEAS CONTEUENCX AT HIMIINGII,II.—The annual conference of the National Union of Elementary Teachers was opened at the Town Han, Birmingham, on Monday, when the delegatte were we coined by the Mayor and the representatives of various educational institutions. The new president, Mr. Wild, referred It• the report of the Royal Commission on Education with a view to pointing out how fully it had supported the complaintsof teachers against the system of payment by results. The Conference was resumed at Birming- ham, on Tuesday, when, in the morning, at a breakfast given by the Mayor, the Bishop of London, who formed one of a &potation from the National Temperance Union, said there was no blot upon the country no black as that of intemperance, and he begged the teachers who heard him to try and influence parents through their children. The teachers !tamed a resolution condemning the retention in the code of payment by results, and also I decided that further legislation with regard to school : attendance was required. At a public meeting held in the Town Hall in the evening, Mr. Chamberlain, who was the principal speaker, expressed his views on several paints connected with elementary schools, and especially on free primary education, a reform which he looked upon as inevitable. On Wednesday the be. A. R. Vardy read a paper on " The Artistic Spirit in Education." div.p: ALDERMAN CROSFIELD AND MR. BRIGHT.

Mr. John Crosfield has made public the following narrative of an interview with the late Mr. John Bright —Whilst the whole notion is mourning over the Math of the great Tribune of the pipit., it may interest your readers, if I narmte as well as lean from natitory, an interview which it was my great privilege to have with John Bright two years ago. I wrote and asked if .1 : might vome and consult him ahout the Irish position. Tle wnge back a very characteristic letter, saying that taunt know his opinions, as he had spoken them la He sutpected that I differed from him, tog if I thought I could change his opinion I waiver). intuit mit- taken. However,he would be glad to see nie. i replied that I should corny to hint at anon to a fatherfor instruc- tion and information. to I went to One Ash, Rochdale, in the early part of 13117. 'the snow was lying three inches deep in the garden as I drove up to his hoot.. I found him writing in his dining-rootn, wi h hit little Scotch terrier by his side. Ile toil, I think I had tatter read two letters I wrote to Mr. Gladstone, as they will give yummy opinions about the Irish question." These letters have woo been published, hist no doubt they will be printed when hit life is written. Ile looked upon them AS sn itnportant that he had kept copies. Ile spoke of Mr. Gladstone in terms of affection, and deep regret that he could not agree with Mr. Gladstone's Irish Bills. John Bright remarked, tt Gladstotio is not infallible—l am not infallible—no man it infallible." Then he told me itf what he coo:Mere," were Gm- stone's mistakes. Ile mentioned the Crialeaa Way, the Egyptian War, be. I said, Mr. Bright, I was educated as you were at • Friends' school, and I agreed all my life in everything you have said or done, and it is very painful to we that I outnot agree with you now on the Irish question." John Bright remarkel I cannot trust the Irish members to have theirown Parliament." Of course I went to learn, not I,' argue, on, I sail nothing except this, "Lord Spencer is an upright mid se.ittle non, and was Lord-Lieutenant of Indent] for nine years, and he approvis of Mr. Glad- stone's; policy, and he has influenced sty opinion bemuse I think he understands the wants of Ireland as well as anyone." John Bright said, I have a very high opinion of Lord Spencer, and I don't wonder he Iran in- fluenced you in this question." I said, Mr. Bright, ,itm told as in the House of Commons force is no rernoly." Ile replied, "No, I said that in Itirminghatn, and say so still." It was not for me to argue with so great a statesman, but I itould not help wondering how lie /timid support lialfitur's coercion as agaitot Glailstone's policy of conciliation. Whild we were conveming, John Bright turned to his little Scotch terrier, and said, with that beautiful smile on his face, Ah ! Fly, thou diet sent trouble thyself with the Irish question." He seemed to dislike and altniAt despise office. Ile skid, t. You have no idea how some men cling to office. They will gothrough almost any degrada- tion rather than be tunnel out." I think he disliked the itleaof being paid as a Cabino Minister. John Bright did not tell toe anything that he would propose to do in place of Home Rule, and I had to leave him convinced dant conciliation is better than coercion. I felt that I had been in the presence of one of the grodest and noblest men that ever lived. I believe at tho time John Bright was inspired, and it Viaa his perfect faith in the Great Supnane and his wonderful eloquence that gave Ilam such a power over his cmintrymen.
PROFESSOR HIGGINS' THE PAR& CHUTIST, AT ST. HELENS.

In the presence of a large, crowd of persons Professor Higgins accomplished a successful balloon ascent and parachute descent on nunKlay night. The iminense concourse of people was unprecislented in St. Helens. Not only did some thousands pay or admission to Grange Park, but the roads about St. Ana's and the Old Toll Bar were also erowiled. It was estimated that no fewerthan 25,000 view,' the performance. The arrangements for ll,' supply of gas MOTO more satisfactory than on former oreasionS, and stout half past six o'clock 1 everything woo mady for the ascent. The monster !balloon woo 1111llt1111 and on ascending it contained shunt 17,000 ft-A of gas. The arrangements were made by Professor who had the assistance of Signor Itellani, a noted balloonist. The parachute ~at orally attracted a groat deal of at tention and scrutiny. It isinsists of alight wickerwork frame,overlapped to the extent of about three feet with a klntl of silk satin material, cut and shaped, when open, like;, prodigious umbrella. The top sill,,- parachute was fastened to the network at tin, side of the balloon by apiece of twine ; wine!, breaks by the Professor's ownwitight as he drops ; burin his balloon. On the words "Let go" from Professor Higgins about 20 strong-looking men who hail been holding it down released the Mots and the hilloon rose steadily in the air, amid the cheers of the assembled thousands. Professor Higgins was observed sitting on a wooden ring Or trapeze at the bottom of the balloon network, with his feet dangling in the air, and in his hands he held a smaller woolen ring attacned to about 20 strings fron the edges of the parachute, which seemed crushed against the aides of the 'saloon. The balloon shot up at a rapid rate. In aboot two minutes Professor Higgins looked but a speck in the sky, and lie afterwards stated that he had ascended about 6,000 feet. .A breathless silence was kept by the crowd. Sod- ; 'hotly the Professor was noticed to drop from 1113 !SOat ; the parachute followed i,, allump, and seemed to ' fall rapidly for a short distance—perhaps 200 feet. Then the parachute gradually opened, and Professor ; Higgins, hanging by his hands, was observed to be makilig Isis descent in a steady and graceful manner. lab-c cheer was raised, and a rush was made for the spot where he alighted---a plough,' field on Knob- stick flat Fenn, 011 the opposite side of the London and North-Western railway at Thatto Heath, situated about half a mile front his ascending point. The time oeciipiol in his:L.7old and descent was iibout five miniitts. He drag,' safely upon his feet, but the ploughed gnound, and his hold upon die parachute, ; caused liiin to slip on his side, without, however, the i slightest accidLit or mohap. The Professor was after- wanbi carried shoulder high by his admirers, to Orange Park, where he addressed the crowd around hini. Ile said he woo glad the rola° of St. Helens could appne cia Ca perfortuance by one of their own countrymen. was sorry they hadl been disappointed up to that , night, hut now that it had bo-a given he hoped the next 5i,,,,- he came he should meet with the same reception I that lie had done that nig,ht. After Professor Higgins ; . . .

left the balbrm, the latter gradually turned over by the weight of the ballast bag attached to the top, and the gas rapidly oiraped. The balhval fell near the old colliery in Elephant-lane and, fortunately, sustained little or no damage. This made the sixth public exhibition ot Professor Iliggi..

'Unworn Football Club brought their season ton successful conclusion on Saturday, when they adminis- tered a severe thrashing to Leeds St. Johns. The first team have only lost four games throughout the wason, and have a record for woring that very few clubs ran equal. Their total wore is 48 goals, 48 tries, and 146 nOnors, whilst their opponents have only worml 6 goals, 12 tries, and 53 minors.

There was a rather rough game at Widnes on Saturday, when the local team met. lleekniondwike. The points were equal at the finish, and the game was declared a draw. In the progress of the match, an unpleasant incident occurred, calling for the interference of the , referee. Wliiist several players were scrambling on the ground, Tobin got his ann round the neck of Williams, and refusivl to let him rise. At length, when he had freed himself, Williamsstruck his ipponent, and in the excited etinditionof affairs the game was suspended. Tin referee thought it his duty to caution both players, and amicable relations were then resumed.

The Good Friday run at the St. Helens Cyclist Club came oft" according to programnw," and was a very successful affair. About thirty members took part in it and altogether they made a very imposing turn-out. Front St. Helena they Caine through Itainhill to War- rington where they excited a good deal of curiosity as they wended their way through the narrow streets of the old town. They did justice to a line repast pre- pared for theta by mine host of the Norton Arms, and then assembling at the call of the bugle, they like , tt giants refrwhed " were again on the road for Hisi , !Green. A retum was made to the Norton Arms tor tea, anal at 8.30 the party set out from Warrington for St. Helens which they reached in due time.

Among the incidents of the run won the plintognimh- ing od the party by one of the members of the club. This devotee of the photographic art likewise took several views en route. Another member of the club amused and ainar.ed the passers-by with his clever antiou on his machine.

THE " BOATING FATALITY ON TRE MERSEY." Sir,—The plucky conduct of the crew of the Deer. foot, who went t, the assustanco of the nine unfortu- nate inside who were plunged into the Mersey through the sinking of the "Sarah Ann "cannot be too highly cannwinihid. Mr. Coroner Brighouse complimented Skelhorn and Boardman iin their conduct when he !Ad the inquest on Saturday, and I am told that he gener- ously gave them something out of his own pocket as a token of his admiration. It is true that perhaps they were not much inconvenienced hy going to the rescue, but it is none the leas a fact that but for their prompt aid several more liven would probably have been lost. They deserve every praise, not only from the Coroner and jury, but from the publie at large. Honour to whom honour is due.—Yours tic,, Warrington, April 23rd, 1889.
LEARN TO SWIM-BUT WHERE ?

div.head: AN ADMIRF:II.
div.p: AN ADMIRF:II.

..... . . . Sir,—The sudden plunging of nine persms into the river on Good Friday, and the prevalence of boating accidentn generally at thin season of the year, serve to still further emphasise the levil that there in that every pertain, male or female, shoshl learn to swim. Whether or not a knowledge of swimming would have resulted in the saving of life when the istastrope happened on the Mersey I do not know, but when accidents of this kind happen—accidents which might inteur to any of Ms—it should impress upon the thinking mind the atsolute necessity of learning how to swim. Again, a person who can swim can often render useful aid in suchemergencien. , white 'lnc who could not would have to stand helplessly ! by. Admitting the necessity of gaining thin useful knowledge, the question of how to do no has to be faced. A person can't very well go to the canals or the river to learn. If he did tie would very likely get drowned, and if he did not get drowned he would be nummoned for trespatin or indecency ; and the only refuge iA the public baths. The baths, however, are altogether inadequate in their accommodation, and it is thc bounden duty .4 the Corporation to go in for a speedy extension. There in a growing demand for increased facilities in this direction, and the municipal authorities must meet it, whatever the cont. Let them give up wrangling about the Town Ilan wall, and give the public what they want. —Toms he. J. 11. April 23rd, 1889.

div.head: CERTIFICATED BOATMEN.
div.p: CERTIFICATED BOATMEN.

Sir,—l should like through your columns to ask sone member if the Town Council to bring before the very nest meeting of that body the desirability, if not the neceasity, of making some pmvision whereby the owners and captains of sailing boats that navigate the Alersev, in the neighbourhood of Warrington, may be required to take out 11.01184'0. I certainly think, and many of my fellow.townspeeple urn of the same opinion, that per- sons who take ceemmanet of those boats should be the holders if some kind of certificates testifying to their capacity and fitness. The std accident of Good Friday shows the, necessity of this. Ido not take it upon my. self tee criticise the management of the captain of thee unfortunate Sarah Ann," as I know nothing alseut sailing myself, but I contend that if certificates wen` i 5911141 it would to' all the better for qualifieal wateremen themselves. so well as doing a deal tn cnsure the safety of the public. As far as I can learn it would be ixisoible for me to him a boat and taken number of friends up the river, but if I inade such an attempt I should dread the result. If, however, I was foolish enough to think of such a thing, I might to be protected from mvsolf, not for my own sake but for the sake of tethers vibes. lives I might put in jeopardy. Ida not wish to blame anyone. in regard to the recent accident, but take advan- tage of a time when public attention has been called to the dangers of the river, to put forward these views. I hope you will insert them, as something should be done. —Yours, Scc., Warrington, April 22nd, 1289.

div.head: DEAR STGAR.-A PROTEST.
div.p: DEAR STGAR.-A PROTEST.

Sir,—Will you kindly grant me space in your columns for the statement of a few facts in connection with the question of Sugar Bounties r The agitation or rather the deception, he., so far as it has gone has had one effect at least—a very unfavourable one to the con- sumers—the price has gone up from 20 to 25 per cent. We have now to pay as much for 6105. of sugar, As we did a fortnight ago for 5155. This mime: a redueed con- sumption or increased expenditure in most families of the working population ; it must be the former. The sugar importers—anticipating the passing of the Bill lately introduced into the House of Commons—for the prohibition into this country of what is Called Bounty-fed Sugar have,most probably by mutual agnsenent,stepped forward and advanced the price, determined to be in time, and,whether the bill passes or not, to get what they can. The reason Assigned for this prohibition, is, as far as I can learn, the protection of the sugar-refining mer- chants who say that,by our buying sugar front countries whew Governments grant a bonus of a certain sum per cwt. upon all rogue exported by their sugar manu- facturers, the sugar refining industry in this country— like inany otter industries—is in a very unprofitable condition, then-fore they urge upon the Government the prohibition of what is called bounty-fed sugar. They are taxing the consumer alnady 25 per cent., and should they succeed with their lull before the saul comes, I have no doubt Use price of sugar will be double what it is at present. This tax will not lament the National Exchequer a farthing, but only the sogar n-finers, who with their workpeople nutrLer 5.000 to 6,000 people. But I ask must Use millions of this country Ise taxed in the article of sugar 100 percent. for the b-nefit of these few pronoun? On the other hand ,there are engaged intim confectionary, preserved fruit, sweets, cordials, temperanee drinks, and a host of other industries, 60,000 to 70,000 persons, who, if this bill passes, will be ruined. Most these 60,000 to 70,000 le mcritieed lathe 5,000 or 6.000? The greatest good of the greatest number should be the object of all legislation. Should this bill become law, that maxim will be reverssl. Should this bill become law, and its evil effects have to be borne, it 'nay tie repealed, but that will not relieve on. We shall by it bind ourselves to °Wier countries, who do not grant a bounty on exported sugar, and without whose consent we carsnot rid tam- s -Imo of this inculsus on our industries and our comfort. ask. Sir, through your columns, the toiling masses of this district—will you allow this Lill to become law Beware of it ; it is the insertion of the thin end of the wedge of Protection. If you submit to this, it is very pmmible that your broad may follow seen, in the landlord's intenat, and why not ten, butter, cheese, meat, or any other artiele tSf food. Working-men and working-women speak out and consign this bill to the oblivion from which it shall never etnerge.-1 ant, Sir, yours respectfully, Sankey Bridges, April 24th, 1869.

div.head: 3IANCHESTEIt SHIP CANAL. NORTON.
div.p: THE 3IANCHESTEIt SHIP CANAL. NORTON.

There is much picturesque scenery in the neighbour- hoial of Norton, which has been invaded by the canal constructor and his men. High up on the right the ancient walls of Halton Castle crown the slope, woods stretch all around ; and sometimes the isanal frays the edge of a wood. The wide earthen track now lies parallel with the river, whose windings soon wander away from the straight course of the canal. All along the line it is flanked by hundreds of acres of spoil ground—green fields that are being covered with raw earth, on which the gra., of future summers may grow again. This brown irruption marks the course of the canal as a feature of the landscape that can he seen Ind. away. Tar distant spectator Set, the earth king with the puffs from engines concealed in the ,uttinq, and dotted with the summits of tall cranes ;old steam navvies. Beside( formidable railway emssings there are other obstacles which break the continuity of the eating. At the beginning of the motion a tiny stream crosses its path, and then the Runcorn and Latchford Canal slants Mon rightto left over it. The first will empty itself into Idle Ship Canal ; and tie. second is now a deserted water- way that will shortly end its days. It is not again met I with until near Warrington, nearly three miles away. For wane distance the men are work.. ing upon the upper layers of clay and sand, Mid have, as yet, only dug their deep truneh. Further on, however, the upper earth has been removed, and a deeesu level reached. Sandstone of a piculiadv rich red haa been struck, and hundreds of tons of it quarriisl. The presence of so moeli solid rock is rhiri I part of the cutting recalls the fact that out of I 6,000,000 cubic yards f excavation to he dime on the , entire section (2,000,000 have already bora removed), I fully ot.half of the material is rock. This deep open- inc in the earth, when. the men standing at the bottion , are walled in on either side by straight preemie., enables Inc, to judge both of the progreui already made and the great anima of labour that ~as yet to be done along the stretch of four and threeemarter miles, which is the extent of the section. Within a short distance of each other three country roads croon thiS deep-eut part of the seetion. At the present in 111111111 l they are Jul over the chisin by wooden bridges; but two of them will stop short at its edge and disappear. A swing 'midge will in future carry the country folk over Gm canal on the middle road, to which the traffic of the throe will be diverted. A recess now being hewn oar 1.1 the stony side of the cutting marks the position of the swing bridge. WARRINGTON AND LATCHFORD.

' Between Warrington and the Ship Canal the Mersey meanders in a serpentine course, throwing out a big loop of ehannel nearly two miles round From the southern edge of Warrington. The outer arch of the loop touches the Ship Canal. At the point of contact the engineer has design,' the Warrington Docks, taking in 22 acrt's of the channel and banks of the Mersey, and diverting that , ; river right across the hoop inn straight course, so that : instead of sweeping round in a half circle, the slow waters will take a short cut over to the other side anti ~it, the old channel there. The cut- ' ting for the river diversion is across a flat marshy field and the excavation is going rapidly on. Leaving the site of the Warrington Docks—which are among the things of the future—thevisitor is on the way to the end of the section at Latchford. The first obstruc- tion is the road leading through Stockton Heath to War- ringlets, which will be continued by a swing bridge over the canal. The canal IRASeS through Stockton Heath, knocking one or two ol,tructive houses ma of the way, and once more entering the green fields. Hen, the cutt- ing is being emptied of its upper layers of rich golden sand. At Latchfitni a great change will come to pass. Hr.,. more an important line of railway crosses thecanal and again the expedient of a deviation railway and a : high bridge is being resorted to. It it the Warrington and Stoekport line of the London and NortieWestern ' Railway Co., and the change occurs awkwardly for the Latchford Station, %Odell will have to be ram' and rebuilt on another site on the deviation railway. Ti,, bridge will be similar in design to the structure already described. The lofty ontranktnents on which it will ntst are now being elevated.
POACHING BY NAVVIES.-A GAMEKEEPER WANTS TO KNOW WHAT TO DO WITH THE DOGS.

James Smith and John (in-en i alias John Heed), two Ship Canal navvies who had lodged at the huts. Thelwall, were. charged on Friday, at Lvinin Petty Sessions, with poaching at High Leigh on the 23rd April. Neither id thee] appeared. John Austin, gamekeeper to Colonel Legit, said that on the day named he saw four men awl a bily mar the big wood, High Leigh. They had two greyhounds with them and he saw them go on to the laud and chase a hare. Witnms with two other men ran down the road when the poachers, being warned by a man on the road, came back to the highway and were then chased by witness and his companion who, after a run of about two wiles, caught Green and Smith. Wheat searched they hind nothing upon them but their tniusers were covered with Wood. The woman, with whom the defendants had lodged, appeared at the court and said the lodgers absconded on the day the summonses were , served, and did not pay her for their last week's lodgings. One of the greyhounds which had been detained by Austin helongerl to her nephew, and in reply to !instill., I who asked what he had LO do with the greyhounds, the ' bench said they mold not advise him on that point. I Austin added that these dogs were constantly being taken about the country by navvies, and especolly on I the Fridays, Saturday., and Sundays. Warrants were I granted for the apprehension of the defendants.

MRS. PARKER'S EMIGRATION SCHEME
We take the following letter from the "Christian World," an.l shall be glad if Mn. Parker will follow with her version ot the facts:—

Sir--If you wish to prevent more young ladies coming here to meet disappointment and want, pray contradict emphatically the many statements made and published by a Mrs. Parker. Three of those she induced to come out, leaving good homes, parents, &c., called on me to-day for advice and help. Their tale of how they have been buffeted about, the., prompts me to pen these lines. Your address line been given me by one of these unfortu- nate girls. Experienced domestic servants can find ready employment here at. from '2O to 50 dollars per month, but not the class of girls Mrs. Parker has induced to come here. I understand there another party of these young ladies now being formed to come hero. I hope this letter may reach you in time to prevent them taking this step. Our good Consul can confirm what I now write if necessary; I am given ID Under:Anon he has already addressed the Department in London on tins subject.--Yours truly, HORATIO BEVERIDGE. San Francisco, April 5.
THE WARRINGTON GYMNASIUM,
COMPETITIONS FOR. MEDALS.

The Committee of the Warrington Gymnasium recently arranged to have two competitions for medals amongst the members, one for the adults and the other for the juniors, and the former came off on Thursday evening in the presence of a con- siderable number of visitors. Amongst those pre- sent were the Mayor (Alderman T. Ii Sutton). Councillor Wright, Mr. Thomas Morrie, Mr. Ferguson, Mr. Dimmelow, Mr. Gorst. Mr. John llesketh, and others. The prizes competed for were a gold centre medal and a silver medal, and there were quite a number of entries. The competition included contests in the following exercises : rings, dumb-bells, bar-hells, horizontal bar, parallel bar, and high jump. Mr. Smith, the able instructor, superintended the exercises and Mr. Alexander. jun., acted as judge. At the conclusion, the judge declared Joseph Podmore to be the winner of the first prize, and George Vernon to be the gainer of the second. The total scores were as follows :- Joseph Po.lmore. 78 marks; George Vernon. 881 ; ! William Podmore, (111 ;2. Holmes, 54 ; G. Thomp on, ; Herbert Hayes, 42; W. Stringer, 41: John A, Chappell, 31; and 2. Macdonald. 25. It should be mentioned that the last-named competitor only took part in a portion of the exercises. The juniors are to have their contest next Tuesday evening. the prizes in this instance being a silver medal and a bronze medal; the latter presented by Mr. Percy Russell. The prizes for both contests will sub- sequently be delivered to the winners.

div.head: CELEBRATION OF A GOLDEN WEDDING AT WA RRINGTON.
div.p: CELEBRATION OF A GOLDEN WEDDING AT WA RRINGTON.

Ti,.. celebration of a golden wedding, in other i word, of fifty years of wedded life, is not a unique, but, in the net tire of things, it is a rare event; and I one which took place in Warrington: on Monday 'evening was tinusually ititeresting in more respects titan one. This was the celebration of the golden wedding of Mr. and Mrs. George Wallington, of Froghall-lane. To mark the occasion, a gathering woo held in the Co-operative Hall, and at this withering there were no fewer than 101 rela- tives of Mr, end Mrs. Wallington present. The company included every one of Mr. Welling. tone childr”it with their wives or husbands, 41 grandchildren, and one great grandchild. The hall , had le.en very nicely decorated for the occasion, and the platform had been fitted up as a kind of , cosy drewing room for the elderly people. A tea, which was catered for by Mrs. Booth, was partaken of, anti afterwards the chair was taken by Mr. John Lowe. During the evening congratulatory addresses were given by the Rev. E. Moore, Mr. M. Walling- ton, Mr. George Wallington, jun., Mr. Edward Wal- lington, Mr. J. Buehler, Mr. John Whittaker, Mr. T. Wallington, and Mr. A. Wellington. The Rey. John Yonne, who was present to tea, was after- wants unexpectedly called away. On behalf of the children every handsome walking stick was pn,- sented to Mr. Wallington by Mr. Daniel Grey, the eldest son-in-law, and a pair of gold-framed spec- tacles to Mrs. Wallington by the youngest daughter, Mrs. England. The epeeches were interspersed with songs by Mrs. Unwin, Mrs. Lowe, Miss E. Wallington, Mr. W. If. Wallington, and Mr. Edmund Wallington. and a pianoforte duet was given by Men. Charles Whittaker and Miss Florrie Whittaker. The children having amused themselves in various games, dancing was afterwards engaged in to music supplied by Mr. Dillon.

div.head: MR. AND MILS. GARNETT'S ORIENTAL TOUR.
div.p: MR. AND MILS. GARNETT'S ORIENTAL TOUR.

Last evening. in the Weeleyan scheedroom at I Penketh, Mrs. R. Garnett delivered a leetnre des- criptive of the recent travels of Mr. and Mrs. Robert Garnett and party in distant lands. The chair Was I occupied by Mr. Charles Parker, and there Was a very large attendance, the schoolroom being crowded. Amongst those present. were Mr. and Mrs. R. Garnett, Mr. and Mrs. C. Parker, the Misses Tingley, Miss Dutton (Moore). Dr. Goraahl, K J. Guest, Godson, Mainley, Summeregill, Ac. After Mr. Parker had made, few opening remarks Mr. Garnett remarked that the party left from I Liverpool, and their first stopping place was Lis- bon. From Mahon they went to Algiers—a wonder ful city—from Algiers they went to Malta, and thence to Alexandra and Cairn, passing by the land of Goshen. After visiting other places, they returned to Alexandra and Malta ) from Malta they travelled to flibralter and from Gibraltar home. Mr. Garnett then read an account in Verse of incinents of the voyage and experiences of life on board ship. in which copious reference was made to passengers and members of the crew. The lines, he explained, were written on the last day or two of the voyage, simply for the perusal of the friends on board, but one friend had asked for a copy and had got the verses printed. Mrs. Garnett gave her narrative in a descriptive and entertaining way, and it was listened to with a large measure of enjoyment. She did not know any nicer way of visiting places, she said, than to go by water. To get on board a ship at Liverpool, and to sail instil muldenly dropped down into an Oriental city was the most surprising and enchant- ing thing that they conld conceive. When one travelled by railway the mind gradually became familiarised to change, but When one atepped off a lanat and alighted suddenly in an Oriental city, it felt liksdropping into a eluipter of the Arabian Nights. There WPM the palm trees and the mosques, the strewn) costumes and bright colours, and the effect 'on the mind was really so embarrassing that one wanted to sit down and look at things instead of conning about sight-seeing. Mrs. Gar- nett then referred to the easy-going habits of the Orientals. their love of haeksheesh, and their cus- toms generally. She also described a visit to a manner), and the manner of worellip of the "howling dervish." and related many incidents, both instruc- tive and amuning of the trip. The interest of the I lecture Wag murk added to by the exhibition of a nerd), of artielen of Oriental use and manufacture, and by the fact that several people had been habited in Oriental costume.

div.head: TIIE EEEEEE MURDER..-A CONFESSION.
div.p: TIIE EEEEEE MURDER..-A CONFESSION.

....... A Dundee correspondent says that great sensation was excited on Thursday on the particulars of Itury's confession of murder becoming known. According to his statement, he and his wife, after returning home drunk, commenced quarrelling about a proposal she made for earning money. In a frenzy of passion he strangled her, and next day proceeded to cut up her • body with a view of throwing the remains, piece by piece, into the river. He sickened, however, at his re- volting work, and to get the remains out of sight packed them in a box. lie spent a week of fearful agony, and St last surrendered to the police, hoping to deceive them by 'miming otl the story oh his wife's suicide, as he had not the nerve to forward the box by railway, lest sus- picion should aroused ant. it 3 41011tOnt,
